Context: Pharisees and Herodians try to trap him: should taxes be paid to Caesar? Audience: hostile questioners. Occasion: a public test designed to force a self-incriminating answer.
Render the following saying (Matthew 22:21) in present-day English, keeping its original force and reasoning:
“Give therefore to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.”
Then give Caesar back what has Caesar's name on it — and give God what belongs to God.

Context: Teaching a crowd anxious about food and clothing. Audience: ordinary listeners. Occasion: addressing worry over daily provision.
Render the following saying (Matthew 6:28-30) in present-day English, keeping its original force and reasoning:
“Why are you anxious about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow. They don’t toil, neither do they spin, yet I tell you that even Solomon in all his glory was not dressed like one of these. But if God so clothes the grass of the field… won’t he much more clothe you?”

Why stress about clothes? Look at the wildflowers in a field. They don't work or sew, yet not even a billionaire in his finest was dressed as well as one of them. If that's how God dresses the grass — here today, cut down tomorrow — don't you think he'll take care of you?

Context: A scribe asks which commandment is the greatest. Audience: a sincere questioner. Occasion: a request to rank the whole law.
Render the following saying (Mark 12:29-31) in present-day English, keeping its original force and reasoning:
“The greatest is… you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart… The second is this, ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ There is no other commandment greater than these.”

The most important one is this: love God with everything you've got — all your heart, all your soul, all your mind, all your strength. And the second is just like it: love the person next to you as much as you love yourself. Nothing outranks these two.
